claims.text: The initial high-entropy nanoalloy has a homogeneous, single-phase structure.
High mixing entropy stabilizes a single-phase solid solution at high temperature.
Nanoscale heterogeneities induce sluggish atomic diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion limits phase separation and chemical segregation.
Finely distributed grain boundaries and defects inhibit rapid atomic diffusion.
High mixing entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for segregation.
The combination of reduced segregation driving force and limited diffusion kinetics mitigates phase separation.
After high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain greater phase stability than a lower-entropy or bulk-alloy baseline.
After high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain greater chemical homogeneity than a lower-entropy or bulk-alloy baseline.
The lower-entropy or larger-grained baseline will undergo more segregation and phase separation under comparable high-temperature conditions.
The prediction applies only in temperature regimes where diffusion remains sufficiently slow because of nanoscale effects.
Extremely high temperatures can enhance diffusion enough to invalidate the proposed stabilization mechanism.
Reactive atmospheres can introduce degradation mechanisms outside the scope of the prediction.
The stabilization magnitude and duration may vary with alloy composition and thermal conditions.
Phase evolution can be assessed using electron diffraction.
Atomic-scale chemical segregation can be assessed using atom probe tomography.
